sources.what: Problem description, competition structure, datasets, performance metric, submission format
sources.note: Confirmed verbatim: metric is a distance-weighted Tversky index with alpha=0.2, beta=0.8; triangular kernel k(d)=max(1-d/R,0) with R=300 m = 3 px at 100 m; TP_w/FP_w/FN_w formulas; the worked example TP=3.00 FP=1.89 FN=2.00 -> 0.60. Submission must be EPSG:32611, 100 m, same bounds, single float32 layer with values in [0,1]. training_features.tif is UTM 11N at 100 m with the 19 listed layers. Initial Prize Round $50k (top 5 x $10k) scored on a private set of expert-labelled new faults; Final Prize Round $250k ($100k/$70k/$40k/$25k/$15k) re-scores the same submissions against an expanded label set built by expert review of every team's submission.
Referenced by the brief; the substantive requirements are on page 967.
Cannot be fetched here without DrivenData credentials, and none are requested or stored. Data is restored from SHA-256-pinned owner mirrors instead - see registry/data_manifest.json.

Top of the public leaderboard at fetch time: #1 nchuzhoy 0.3262, #2 kinghorton42 0.3222, #3 alexoktaba 0.3220, #4 DARD 0.3195, #5 joeyfezster 0.3163. The 0.3195 quoted in the brief was #4, not #1; the current leader is 0.3262. Our own family best (extradr19, 0.2778) sits at #13.

sources.what: ORGANISER ANSWER - known USGS/INGENIOUS faults are masked out of scoring
sources.verified: yes - posts 2 and 4, user chrisk-dd, DrivenData Staff
sources.note: Verbatim, post 2 (Sep 16): 'Pixels corresponding to known USGS/INGENIOUS faults are masked / excluded from evaluation, so they do not count towards penalty terms.' and 'Re-evaluation will also mask/exclude the existing USGS/INGENIOUS faults.'  Verbatim, post 4 (Sep 21): 'The mask is indeed pixel-exact - it is identical to the provided set of training fault labels.'  The same post notes that new-fault ground truth may lie within 300 m of a known trace and that finding those is 'one outcome we are aiming for'.  Consequence: emitting on a known fault is neutral - no credit, no penalty - but it consumes emission budget, and predictions near a known trace ARE fully penalised.  Implemented as the pixel-exact `known` mask in gems42.metric and as exclude=labels in the emission selector.

sources.what: ORGANISER ANSWER - test-set construction will not be disclosed
sources.verified: yes - post 7, user chrisk-dd, DrivenData Staff, Sep 23
sources.note: Verbatim: 'We're not sharing details about the data sources, fault types, or coverage behind the test faults beyond what's in the problem description.' Also: 'the largest prize pool (Phase 2) will use a test set that is updated by expert review of all Phase 1 submissions, so your fault predictions have an impact on final evaluation even if they are not the most performant in Phase 1.' So no leakage about test-set construction is available to anyone, and Phase 2 rewards defensible geological discovery, not only Phase 1 rank.

sources.what: Hornby, Boschetti & Horowitz (1999), Analysis of potential field data in the wavelet domain, GJI 137(1) 175-196
sources.verified: yes - abstract read via the OUP landing page
sources.note: Confirms the method's basis: Green's functions from Poisson potential theory build continuous wavelets; this yields relations between horizontal derivatives of the field at all heights and the wavelet transform of the zero-height field; maxima of the wavelet transform are the multiscale edges. Keywords on the record: 'gravity anomalies, magnetic anomalies, multiscale edge analysis'.

sources.what: Archibald, Gow & Boschetti (1999), Multiscale edge analysis of potential field data, Exploration Geophysics 30(1-2) 38-44
sources.note: This is the 'worm map' paper (the phrase 'worm maps' appears in its abstract). Used here for the documented fact that the trace of a gradient maximum migrates in the direction of dip under upward continuation, which is why gems42.worming tolerates lateral migration between continuation levels instead of demanding a fixed pixel.

sources.what: Horowitz (2018), Potential Field Poisson Wavelet Multiscale Edge Analysis, Stanford Geothermal Workshop
sources.note: The operational recipe implemented in gems42/worming.py, quoted verbatim: 'the worm technique from original Hornby et al. (1999) paper takes a Bouguer gravity grid, upward continues it to a suite of heights, then detects local maxima in the horizontal gradient of the results at each height, marking those locations as multiscale edges. Hornby et al. (1999) show that - to within a factor - upward continuation *is* a wavelet scale change.' Also confirms the multiscale edges are local peaks of the horizontal-dipole source density, whose geological reading is steeply dipping contacts.
